stem: A compliance team is building a system whose requirements are fixed by statute, must be exhaustively documented before a single line of code is written, and cannot legally change mid-project without a formal amendment. A junior PM proposes running the work in two-week sprints anyway, arguing agile is 'just better.' What is the strongest argument against her proposal?
options: Adaptive approaches cannot produce any documentation at all, which regulators require
Adaptive approaches trade formal upfront control and thin documentation for fast feedback — a poor exchange when scope is already fixed and documentation must satisfy a regulator, not a customer
Sprints are always longer than a month, which regulators forbid
Scrum Masters are not legally permitted to work on regulated projects
explanation: Adaptive's honest weaknesses are thin governance/documentation and reliance on scope flexing through the backlog. When scope is already fixed by law and documentation must satisfy an external regulator rather than a paying customer, agile's core advantages (fast feedback, flexible scope) buy nothing while its weaknesses (lighter formal control) become liabilities. It is a fit argument, not a legal or procedural fabrication.

stem: A startup is building a consumer app where the founders openly admit they don't yet know which features customers will actually use, the market shifts monthly, and the team can ship a usable slice every two weeks. A board member insists on a comprehensive requirements document and a fixed baseline before any coding starts. What is the strongest argument against the board member's approach?
options: A predictive baseline built on genuinely unknowable requirements locks in guesses early and defers discovery of errors to the point where they are most expensive to fix
Predictive approaches are illegal for consumer software
A requirements document always takes longer to write than the entire project
Board members are never permitted to set project constraints
explanation: Predictive's honest weakness is that feedback arrives late and change is expensive once baselined. When requirements are genuinely unknowable up front — the startup's actual situation — a predictive baseline is a guess dressed as certainty, and errors in that guess surface only after the expensive commitment is made. This is the textbook profile for an adaptive approach instead.

stem: A team is fully distributed across three time zones with no shared office. For this virtual team to run Scrum successfully, what must the organization deliberately supply that a colocated team gets for free?
options: Nothing — virtual teams cannot practice agile under any circumstances
Modern collaboration tooling and explicit working agreements about communication and overlap hours
A single scrum master physically present with each subgroup at all times
A predictive baseline to compensate for the lack of face-to-face contact
explanation: Virtual teams can run agile well, but the organization must deliberately build what colocation provides automatically: collaboration technology and disciplined working agreements about availability and communication. Virtual is not inherently agile-hostile — it is agile-hostile only without that scaffolding.

stem: A Scrum team routinely fails to complete its sprint commitments because two of its five developers are functional employees who get pulled onto other departmental priorities mid-sprint by their functional manager. Which organizational-structure factor best explains this recurring failure?
options: A weak matrix structure, where functional managers retain authority over people's time and undermine the dedicated, stable membership adaptive teams require
A strong project-oriented structure, which is ideal for agile delivery
A hierarchical structure, which has no bearing on team staffing
A virtual team structure, which always causes missed commitments
explanation: In a weak matrix, functional managers hold the real authority over resource time, so team members get pulled onto competing priorities — exactly the decentralized-portfolio problem that poisons sprint commitments. A strong matrix or dedicated project structure would grant the team real authority over its own members' time instead.

stem: Which enterprise environmental factor (EEF) most directly facilitates an organization's adoption of adaptive approaches?
options: A culture of trust and safety that tolerates failure as a source of learning
A change-control board that requires six weeks to approve any adjustment
Documentation standards written exclusively for predictive projects
Departmental silos that keep specialists reporting through separate chains
explanation: A culture of trust and safety, with tolerance for failure as learning, is a facilitative EEF that lets teams experiment, inspect, and adapt without fear of blame. The other three options are the hostile versions of organizational assets — the kind a servant leader has to reform, not lean on.

stem: Which organizational process asset (OPA) actively suppresses an organization's ability to adopt adaptive approaches?
options: An agile-friendly PMO offering coaching, training, and tool templates
A library of existing team charters and working agreements
A formal change-control process built for predictive baselines that takes six weeks to approve any adjustment
Escalation paths designed for rapid impediment removal
explanation: A change-control process designed for a fixed predictive baseline is exactly the kind of hostile OPA that blocks agility — it forces the fast feedback loops of an adaptive project through a process built for the opposite cadence. The other three are facilitative OPAs the Practice Guide names explicitly.

stem: Ordering the logical units of adaptive work from LARGEST to SMALLEST, which sequence is correct?
options: Task, story, iteration, epic, release
Release, epic, iteration, story, task
Epic, release, task, story, iteration
Story, task, release, epic, iteration
explanation: A release bundles multiple iterations (sprints); a large epic is bigger than any single iteration because it takes several iterations' worth of stories to complete; within one iteration, the team finishes user stories sized to fit that timebox, and each story decomposes further into technical tasks. Release > epic > iteration > story > task.

stem: During backlog refinement, the team discovers that a single backlog item is far too large to realistically finish within one two-week sprint. What is the correct response?
options: Extend the sprint's timebox until the item can be finished
Split the oversized item (the epic) into smaller user stories that each fit within the fixed iteration
Assign the entire item to one developer to work on across several sprints without splitting it
Remove the item from the backlog permanently since it cannot be estimated
explanation: The iteration's timebox is fixed and does not stretch to accommodate oversized work; instead the unit of work is split — an epic becomes smaller stories that fit inside the sprint. Bending the timebox to the work item, rather than the reverse, is the recurring exam trap here.

stem: Which statement correctly identifies a genuine trade-off of using a fixed iteration (timebox) rather than an open-ended work period?
options: Timeboxes guarantee that every planned item will be finished by the deadline
A timebox creates a regular cadence for feedback and forecasting, but work that doesn't fit must be deferred or split rather than let the box grow
Timeboxes eliminate the need for backlog refinement entirely
Timeboxes are only usable by teams larger than fifty people
explanation: The benefit of a fixed timebox is a predictable cadence for planning, delivery, and feedback (and it enables velocity as a forecasting tool); the cost is that scope, not time, must flex — unfinished or oversized work is deferred or split, never used as a reason to lengthen the iteration.

stem: A predictive WBS contains the work package 'Design and build customer login module,' estimated at six weeks of effort. The team is moving to two-week sprints. What is the correct way to translate this work package into the adaptive plan?
options: Keep it as a single six-week work package and pause sprints until it's finished
Split it into multiple smaller user stories (e.g., password reset, social sign-in, session timeout) that each fit inside a single sprint, ordered in the backlog by value
Convert it directly into one Daily Scrum agenda item
Discard it, since WBS work packages have no adaptive equivalent
explanation: Translating a WBS to an adaptive plan means work packages become backlog items or user stories, split until each fits inside one iteration, then ordered in the backlog by value. A six-week package cannot become a single sprint's story — it must be decomposed.

stem: While translating a WBS into backlog items, the team encounters a work package whose technical approach is genuinely unknown — nobody can estimate it with any confidence. What is the appropriate adaptive technique for handling it?
options: Assign it the same story-point estimate as a similar-looking, well-understood item
Create a spike: a short, timeboxed investigation whose output is the knowledge needed to estimate and split the real work
Escalate it to the sponsor to be removed from scope permanently
Skip estimation and add it directly to the current sprint at full size
explanation: A spike is a timeboxed investigation used specifically when a backlog item hides unknowns that block confident estimation or splitting. Its output is information, not a shippable increment, and it converts an unknown into stories the team can actually plan.

stem: In adaptive planning, scope for the release is continuously assembled from which set of living inputs?
options: A single signed-off requirements specification and nothing else
The project charter/vision, the product roadmap, personas and customer voice, and previously refined backlog items
Only the sprint backlog from the immediately prior sprint
The organization's annual budget document
explanation: Unlike predictive planning's single requirements baseline, adaptive scope is re-derived every cycle from several living sources: the charter/vision, the roadmap, personas/customer voice, and backlog items carried forward from prior refinement — continuously converted into ready stories.

stem: A new Product Owner skips writing a product vision or roadmap and jumps straight to drafting sprint backlogs from scratch each sprint. What problem does this create?
options: None — sprint backlogs are the only scope input an adaptive team needs

Without a vision and roadmap feeding backlog refinement, the team loses the directional inputs that let it prioritize consistently across sprints, risking a backlog that reacts to whichever request is loudest rather than what delivers the most value
It violates PMI's rule that all projects must use a WBS
It automatically converts the project to a predictive life cycle
explanation: The sprint backlog is refinement's output, not scope's input. Skipping the vision and roadmap removes the directional inputs that anchor consistent, value-based prioritization, leaving the team to react to noise rather than pursue a coherent release direction.

stem: Which of the following is an ARTIFACT used on an adaptive project, as opposed to an event or a role?
options: The Daily Scrum
The Sprint Retrospective
The Product Backlog
The Scrum Master
explanation: The Product Backlog is one of Scrum's three artifacts (with the Sprint Backlog and the Increment). The Daily Scrum and Sprint Retrospective are timeboxed events; the Scrum Master is a role, not an artifact.

stem: A team disagrees at the end of a sprint about whether a story is truly finished — one developer says it's done because the code compiles, another says testing and documentation are still outstanding. Which artifact exists specifically to prevent this disagreement?
options: The product roadmap
The Definition of Done — a shared quality checklist every increment must satisfy
The sprint burndown chart
The team's velocity history
explanation: The Definition of Done is the adaptive artifact that establishes an agreed, shared checklist for what 'finished' means at the story/increment level, precisely to prevent exactly this kind of disagreement between team members.

stem: A team wants to determine whether a completed backlog item can be counted as truly finished. Which criterion correctly answers that question on an adaptive project?
options: Whether the item was completed on the day originally forecast
Whether the item satisfies its acceptance criteria and the team's Definition of Done
Whether the item's actual cost matched its budgeted cost
Whether the item appears on the original project charter
explanation: Success at the task/story level in an adaptive project is defined empirically: acceptance criteria plus the team's Definition of Done, not adherence to a predictive date or cost baseline that adaptive projects don't fix the same way.

stem: How does adaptive project success differ from predictive project success?
options: Adaptive success is measured only by finishing exactly on the original baseline date
Adaptive success is redefined around value delivered — working increments, satisfied customers, sustainable pace, and improving flow — rather than on-time/on-budget/in-scope
There is no way to measure success on an adaptive project
Adaptive and predictive success criteria are identical in every respect
explanation: Predictive success is the classic triple-constraint (on time, on budget, in scope). Adaptive success is redefined around delivered value: working increments, customer satisfaction, sustainable pace, improving flow, and demonstrable quality — evidence-based rather than baseline-based.

stem: A Product Owner is prioritizing a backlog and wants to identify which features will genuinely delight customers versus which are baseline expectations that cause dissatisfaction only if missing. Which prioritization technique should she use?
options: MoSCoW (Must/Should/Could/Won't)
Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF)
The Kano model, which classifies features as delighters, performance features, and must-be basics
A simple first-in-first-out queue
explanation: The Kano model is built exactly for this judgment: it classifies features by their effect on customer satisfaction — delighters, linear performance features, and must-be basics whose absence causes dissatisfaction. MoSCoW sorts by necessity and WSJF sequences by economic cost of delay, neither of which targets the delight-versus-basic distinction.
